one_liner: Python-traced copy-and-patch compiler for small realtime numeric graphs; beats NumPy 2.3.5 per-call overhead by 1.7-3.9x.
what_it_does: You write Python against Copapy types (cp.value, cp.vector, matrices, quaternions, cp.grad for reverse-mode autodiff); Copapy traces this into an acyclic graph, Target().compile(...) turns it into machine code, tg.run() executes it and tg.read_value() fetches results. A @cp.jit decorator wraps ordinary functions and caches the compiled version. The code runs either in-process through a Python C extension or on a separate C runner (realtime Linux thread, RTOS or bare-metal MCU); it is a separate embedded DSL, not a NumPy drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: Copy-and-patch compilation: every graph operation maps to a stencil precompiled by GCC (machine code with relocation holes), the compiler concatenates stencils, strips each stencil's trailing tail-call jmp (an add becomes one addss instruction) and keeps operands in two virtual registers mapped to hardware registers; the runner mmaps code and data, applies architecture-neutral patch records and jumps to the entry point. The whole traced graph runs as one native call, so Python pays one call per evaluation where the NumPy version pays three calls plus temporaries. Tracing also folds compile-time constants and removes multiplications by 1, additions of 0 and branches multiplied by 0.
when_to_use: Small fixed-structure numeric kernels (tens to a few hundred scalars) evaluated at high rate from Python, where NumPy's per-call overhead (about 7.7 microseconds per iteration in the README benchmark) dominates.

Embedded or realtime targets that need deterministic machine code with no syscalls, no libc and memory needs known at compile time: x86_64, x86, AArch64, ARMv6/7 including Thumb and Cortex-M, RISC-V RV32/RV64 with hardware floating point.
Realtime optimisation loops that need reverse-mode autodiff inside the compiled code, such as the README's Madgwick IMU fusion and two-joint inverse kinematics examples.
Graphs with many compile-time constants or sparse (zero) coefficients, which the tracer folds away before code generation.
when_not_to_use: Bulk array math: there are no SIMD stencils yet, the lead drops from about 3.9x at 10 elements to 1.7x at 500, and nothing beyond 500 elements was measured.
Code with data-dependent control flow: branches must be decidable at trace time (cp.iif is the workaround), so general Python programs do not compile.
Workloads that move much data between Python and compiled code: write_value and read_value make one runner call per scalar, and the README benchmark measures no data transfer at all.
Production systems that need stability or hardware I/O: the project is at version 0.0.x, hardware I/O is not yet available, and divide-by-zero is still possible at runtime (README footnote).

integration.form: module (pure-Python compiler plus a C extension runner; stencils ship as per-architecture ELF object files)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime (pyproject lists no dependencies); building from source needs a C compiler, and rebuilding stencils needs GCC plus pelfy (dev extra) via tools/build.sh
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.10+; GCC with tail-call optimisation for stencils (the only supported stencil compiler)
integration.platforms: PyPI 0.0.7.post0 wheels for CPython 3.10-3.14 on Linux x86_64, aarch64 and armv7l (glibc and musl), Windows x86_64 and macOS x86_64/universal2; generated code for x86_64, x86, AArch64, ARMv6/7 (incl. Thumb, Cortex-M) and RISC-V
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Each Target owns its own runner context; the C extension releases the GIL while it executes commands and takes no lock, so sharing one Target between threads is unsafe; the @cp.jit cache is an unlocked module-level dict.

gotchas: Side effects inside assert statements: Target.compile, run and write_value call the runner only inside 'assert coparun(...) > 0' (src/copapy/_target.py), so under 'python -O' or PYTHONOPTIMIZE nothing is compiled or executed and a timing loop like tests/benchmark.py would time a no-op; runner error codes (-4 code and data more than 2 GB apart, -5 bad patch) are also silently dropped then.

@cp.jit caches by function object only: later calls with a different argument count, vector length or type reuse the first trace (zip silently truncates mismatched inputs), and any Python control flow is frozen at the first trace.

README benchmark harness: the Copapy loop never reads its result back while NumPy returns a scalar each iteration; the NumPy case adds an int32 [10,1] array to float32 vectors, which NumPy promotes to float64, so the baseline allocates and computes a 10 x v_size float64 temporary per call while Copapy uses C float; the results JSON is not committed and the unplotted pure-Python row runs 300 iterations but records 3000. The ratio measures call overhead, not code quality.

Early-stage code: wrong-result bugs were closed only in September 2026 (#29 runner built on Windows x64 with /O2, #28 cp.sin on 32-bit x86), after the last non-dev PyPI release (0.0.7.post0, 2026-04-05); the C runner does no bounds checks on COPY_DATA, COPY_CODE or PATCH offsets, so it trusts whatever command stream it receives.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: CPython's copy-and-patch JIT, PochiVM and WasmNow use the same technique for whole languages, C++ metaprograms or Wasm, and Numba or Hana Jit speed up ordinary Python/NumPy on desktops. Pick Copapy only when the output must be deterministic, libc-free machine code for embedded or realtime targets authored from Python, ideally with autodiff; for general numeric speedups Numba covers far more of Python and NumPy.
verified_claims_summary: A first-party chart (README, generated by tests/benchmark.py on a Ryzen 5 3400G against NumPy 2.3.5) shows 30,000 evaluations of sum((v1 + i) @ v2 for i in range(10)) taking about 0.079 s for Copapy versus 0.308 s for NumPy at 10 elements (3.9x) down to 0.321 s versus 0.555 s at 500 elements (1.7x), values read from the SVG markers (derived from page data). The constant gap of about 7.7 microseconds per iteration is NumPy's three-call overhead; GCC version, Python version and whether the PyPI wheel or a local build was used are not stated.
status_note: Active (544 commits, last commit 2026-09-30, 76 stars, no open issues), MIT-licensed and installable from PyPI (0.0.7.post0 stable, 0.0.8 dev pre-release 2026-09-25), but experimental 0.0.x software whose only performance evidence is a self-run chart against NumPy call overhead.
